title: MYP Arts Revision: A Practical eAssessment Plan
summary: MYP Arts revision made practical: learn what to practise, self-assess with criteria A-D, manage ePortfolio time, and build stronger evidence each week.
body_markdown:
MYP Arts revision means improving your artistic process, preserving evidence, and explaining decisions clearly in an ePortfolio. Preparation should combine practical work, focused research, and reflection against the assessment criteria.


A polished artwork or performance may attract attention, but your portfolio must also show how you investigated, experimented, developed an intention, and evaluated the result. The useful habit is simple: make something, record what happened, and decide what to improve.


Start with RevisionDojo's guide to[what the MYP ePortfolio is](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-is-the-myp-eportfolio) . Arts uses an ePortfolio rather than an on-screen examination. Teachers mark the work, which is externally moderated to support consistent standards.


### Your MYP Arts revision checklist


Build your preparation around these priorities:


- Read your session-specific unit, instructions, and criteria.
- Investigate relevant artists, genres, movements, or performances.
- Save practical experiments and explain subsequent decisions.
- Connect techniques and outcomes to an artistic intention.
- Evaluate your work using specific evidence.
- Organise sources and files throughout the project.


Evidence differs across visual art, media, dance, drama, and music. Review[MYP ePortfolio subjects and expectations](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-myp-certificate-eportfolio-subjects-and-what-to-expect) , then follow your school's instructions for your assessment session.


### Understand what Arts eAssessment measures


The MYP Arts framework has four criteria:


Criterion Central focus Evidence to practise producing


A: Investigating Understanding art movements, genres, artworks, or performances Focused research, analysis, and relevant vocabulary


B: Developing Exploring techniques, ideas, and artistic intentions Experiments, rehearsals, annotations, and justified decisions


C: Creating or performing Demonstrating skills in a final outcome Suitable visual, audio, or video evidence


D: Evaluating Reflecting on your work and artistic development Judgments supported by intentions, choices, and examples


These criteria connect. Investigation should influence experimentation; experimentation should shape the outcome; evaluation should judge its effectiveness. Read[how MYP eAssessment works](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-does-myp-eassessment-work) for wider context, while treating your school's session materials as the authority for your task.


### What to practise each week


### Turn investigation into artistic decisions


Research becomes useful when it changes what you make. Select relevant works and ask: which formal choices create an effect, how does context influence meaning, and which technique could I test?


A visual art student might examine composition or texture. A drama student might investigate gesture or staging. A music student could explore rhythm or instrumentation. In each case, explain how the research informs your intention.


RevisionDojo's[MYP Individuals and Societies resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/myp/myp-individuals-and-societies) can support contextual understanding. Keep that context relevant to the artistic choices you analyse.


### Make experimentation visible


Save selected sketches, rehearsal clips, drafts, storyboards, or material tests. After each meaningful experiment, record what you tested, what happened, what you learned, and what you will change.


“I tried charcoal” reports activity. A stronger annotation explains consequence: “Charcoal created the tonal contrast I wanted, but obscured the gesture, so I will combine broad shading with controlled lines.”


The iterative thinking familiar from[MYP Design](https://www.revisiondojo.com/myp/myp-design) also helps here: testing should lead to documented improvements. RevisionDojo Study Notes, Flashcards, and AI Chat can support terminology review. Use Coursework Library examples to consider organisation while keeping submitted work and reflection your own.


### Rehearse under realistic limits


Try a 30-minute technique drill, a timed rehearsal, or a small version of a larger idea. Record what slows you down and whether your technique supports your intention.


Feedback should identify a next action. Ask your teacher or a Tutor where control weakens or an explanation becomes vague, following your school's rules on assistance.

*Two students confront the hidden complexity of creative file management.*


### Self-assess against evidence


Replace “Is this good?” with “What evidence supports this criterion, and where can the assessor find it?” That question turns uncertainty into an editing task.


Check whether research influences later choices, experiments show development, and the final outcome communicates your intention. For evaluation, replace broad statements with references to a specific feature, moment, technique, or feedback comment.


Read the command terms in your teacher's descriptors carefully. Describing a decision and evaluating its effectiveness require different responses. Match your evidence to the descriptors, then explain why it fits. Grading tools can prompt closer review, but use your teacher's criteria and feedback to guide final judgments.


### A four-week preparation plan


Adapt this schedule to your school's deadlines and permitted working arrangements.


When Main priority


Four weeks before submission Read requirements, organise folders, investigate, and begin practical trials


Three weeks before submission Select promising experiments, refine your intention, and develop the work


Two weeks before submission Complete a substantial version, seek permitted feedback, and prioritise improvements


Final week Finish evaluation, check citations, export files, and test playback or access


Use 40-minute blocks with one defined outcome: analyse one artwork, test one technique, or revise one evaluation paragraph. Leave room for practical setbacks rather than scheduling every minute.


Check[which subjects have MYP eAssessment](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-subjects-have-myp-eassessment) when coordinating deadlines. Predicted Papers and Mock Exams can support on-screen subjects; Arts preparation needs sustained practical work and portfolio evidence.


### Build a clear trail of development


Capture experiments as they happen. Name files by stage and date, keep citations beside research notes, and explain rejected options when they reveal meaningful development. Select evidence that makes your progression easy to follow.


RevisionDojo's[MYP eAssessment preparation platform guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/study-platforms-myp-eassessment-prep) helps you coordinate Questionbank practice for other subjects with Study Notes, Flashcards, AI Chat, Grading tools, Coursework Library guidance, and Tutors.


Strong Arts preparation grows through repeated acts of making, recording, judging, and improving. With your teacher's instructions guiding the task and RevisionDojo supporting your wider study routine, the portfolio can become a clear account of your development as an artist.
